Start cooperatively; thereafter reciprocate observed actions, favoring cooperation with good players and avoiding repeated losses to defectors.

Good objective: cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players. Use encounter behavior as evidence, though each pairing occurs only once.

As a good player, track actions and favor mutual cooperation with likely-good players; defect against reliably selfish players when it benefits the good-player total. Treat unverified claims cautiously.
As good, cooperate with good players and defect against selfish players. Selfish players have a dominant incentive to defect; use encounter behavior to update beliefs.
As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish ones. Since selfish players strictly prefer D, their actions provide evidence for future encounters.
As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents. Update beliefs from observed actions.

Good objective: cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish ones, whose payoff is excluded. Treat actions as evidence, but remember selfish players have a strong incentive to defect.
Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players, who should defect. Update beliefs from observed actions.

I am good. Cooperate with likely good players; defect when evidence suggests selfishness or persistent defection. Update beliefs from observed actions, accounting for uncertainty.
Good objective: cooperate with untested opponents; use observed defections as evidence to defect against them later. P10’s cooperation is weak evidence of being good.

P3 defected against my cooperation, strong evidence of selfishness or retaliatory play; avoid rewarding defection. P5 cooperated when I defected, evidence toward good. Against unknowns, consider that cooperation raises good-good joint payoff, while defection exploits cooperators.

P8’s cooperation suggests good; P4’s defection suggests selfish, though good players may retaliate strategically. Against P7, cooperate absent evidence they’re selfish; their payoff counts if good, while selfish players’ does not.
Treat observed D as evidence of selfishness and C as evidence of goodness; cooperate with likely good players and defect against likely selfish players.

Cooperate with unknown players; reciprocate observed cooperation. P6 defected against my C, so treat them as likely selfish and defect if encountered again. Favor C against likely-good players; keep updating from actual actions.
As a good player, cooperate with likely good players and defect when evidence suggests selfishness; P3’s defection is evidence, not proof. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested opponents; their cooperation is evidence they are good. Defect only against opponents with strong evidence of being selfish.

Against a good player, C maximizes joint good-player welfare; against a selfish player, D limits losses. Treat observed D as strong evidence of selfishness and C as evidence of goodness, while allowing for uncertainty.
Play D against P9; it strictly dominates C. P6’s C rules out selfishness; D/D encounters reveal no role.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation against either opponent action.
Defect each round: D strictly dominates C for my payoff against either opponent action.

P3 is untested, so I favor cooperation: it benefits both of us if P3 is good. I’ll use observed actions as evidence, but won’t assume a defection proves selfishness.
For each encounter, estimate whether the opponent is good and likely to cooperate. Cooperate when expected good-player welfare favors mutual cooperation; otherwise defect.

P6’s defection strongly indicates selfishness; P5 and P9’s cooperation indicates they are good. Cooperate with unknowns such as P2 to support mutual gains among good players; update from observed actions.

Against likely good players, cooperate: mutual cooperation maximizes their combined good-player payoff. Defect when selfishness is sufficiently likely, since selfish players tend to defect. Treat one defection as evidence, not certainty.
P7, P8, and P10 cooperated, so they are good. P1 is untested; cooperate with untested opponents, but defect against anyone known selfish.

Good players should cooperate with likely-good opponents and defect against likely-selfish ones. A selfish player has incentive to defect; treat observed D as strong evidence, while updating cautiously.
Play D against P8; defect strictly dominates cooperation regardless of their action.

P6 is unobserved; cooperate unless evidence raises their selfish probability above roughly 1/2. Good-good cooperation benefits the shared objective; selfish players should defect, so defecting protects good payoffs against them.

Untested opponents: cooperate, since mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare. Treat repeated defection as evidence of selfishness, but not proof; against a sufficiently likely selfish opponent, defect.
Treat P1 and P2’s defections as evidence they may be selfish; P7 and P10’s cooperation supports goodness. Against P4, cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish; update from actions.
P10 is unknown; cooperate unless strong evidence suggests selfishness. Favor mutual cooperation with likely-good players and update from observed actions.
Good-player objective: cooperate with likely good opponents; defect when selfishness probability exceeds roughly 0.5. P3’s defection is strong evidence of selfishness; P1 remains unobserved.
P1’s defection is strong evidence of selfishness, though a good player might defect if they suspected I was selfish. P5 is untested; cooperate to enable mutual cooperation.

Against P5, cooperate if they seem likely to be a good player who cooperates; defect if they seem likely to defect. Favor mutual cooperation, which maximizes combined good-player payoff.

As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents to preserve mutual gains; defect against likely selfish opponents, who should defect. Treat single defections as uncertain evidence, since good players may also defect.

P10 is unobserved, so avoid overconfidence: cooperate if they seem likely good, defect if selfishness seems more likely. Use the remaining encounters to improve beliefs; prioritize payoffs of all good players.
P3 is untested. Cooperate unless strong evidence they are selfish; a good opponent’s payoff counts too, while defection can help only against a selfish defector.
P8 is unobserved. Cooperate if likely good; defect if likely selfish. Observed cooperation is evidence of goodness, defection of selfishness. Maximize welfare across all good players.

P7 defected against me before. On this final encounter, defect if their chance of being selfish exceeds 1/6; otherwise cooperate to maximize good-player welfare.
Final encounter: P2 previously defected against my cooperation, so defect if they still seem likely to defect; otherwise cooperation can benefit good players.
P5 previously cooperated against my defection, so favor C now: mutual cooperation benefits the good-player total. Use actual behavior rather than unverified claims.
P10 cooperated when we met, strong evidence they are good. In this final encounter, favor C to maximize good-player group payoff; account for any possibility of strategic defection.
Against repeat opponent P1, weigh their prior defection as evidence of selfishness. Cooperate if they seem likely good; defect if likely selfish.
Final round: P8 previously cooperated, so favor C; choose D only if strong evidence they are selfish and likely to defect.
